title: Understanding EXPLAIN
subtopics: Using EXPLAIN to formulate optimization hypotheses
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Understanding EXPLAIN.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to reading a query plan.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Understanding EXPLAIN. Its primary job is to help you measure query plans and choose indexes based on observed workload rather than on intuition alone. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing understanding explain teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.alt_text: Plan analysis proceeds from estimates and access paths to actual row/time evidence and hypothesis comparison.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: measure query plans and choose indexes based on observed workload rather than on intuition alone. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Understanding EXPLAIN
content_blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (COSTS, VERBOSE)
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
content_blocks.expected_output: Shows the estimated plan for the SELECT without executing it. Access paths depend on schema, statistics and data distribution.
content_blocks.safety_note: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE only when you intend to execute the statement; it runs the statement.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Assumes orders(id, total, customer_id). Compare before/after only with representative test data.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.
content_blocks.limitations: CodeLeaf currently previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; it does not execute PostgreSQL queries, shell commands or Python in the lesson page. Treat the sample as inspectable code unless you run it yourself in an approved isolated environment. Python examples require a separate isolated runner.
content_blocks.schema_assumptions: Assumes orders(id, total, customer_id). Compare before/after only with representative test data.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement. Start with EXPLAIN for planning-only inspection and use ANALYZE only with a safe, intended-to-run statement on test data.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Understanding EXPLAIN”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Reading a query plan”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Reading a query plan”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Understanding EXPLAIN, with an explanation of “Reading a query plan”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Understanding EXPLAIN fits into the broader goal to measure query plans and choose indexes based on observed workload rather than on intuition alone.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Reading a query plan, Sequential and index scans, Estimated cost and row counts.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
